# Prevent information exposure through APIs

## What This Skill Does
This skill reduces Information Exposure (CWE-200 / P96) in C-based API and service code by replacing full-record or generic response serialization with explicit endpoint response builders, limiting routing to registered handlers only, and validating that success and error payloads match an approved contract before return. Use it when code builds JSON directly from internal structs, reuses database-shaped models as API responses, or still exposes deprecated routes.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| A handler serializes a full internal struct with `snprintf(...)` or similar | Apply an endpoint-specific response builder that emits only approved fields |
| Routing dispatches requests through ad hoc path matching or fallback handlers | Replace with an explicit `RouteEntry` allowlist and a fixed not-found response for unknown paths |
| A response may vary by caller role or authorization | Add a per-endpoint field allowlist and validate the final payload against the authorized contract before returning |
| Error responses include internal details, debug text, or unexpected fields | Replace with a fixed error contract and validate error payload shape too |
| Code already maps internal records to response views/DTOs and validates payload fields | No action needed |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Replace full-object API responses with explicit view structs or field-by-field response builders
- Restrict dispatch to registered routes and make unknown routes return one fixed not-found body
- Add simple contract checks for required and forbidden JSON fields before returning a response

### Cannot Do
- Infer business-approved fields without an endpoint contract, tests, or clear caller requirements
- Guarantee JSON correctness or authorization correctness if the application uses custom parsers or undocumented response formats
- Remove every exposure path outside the API response layer, such as logs, core dumps, or database replication outputs

## Gotchas
- Hiding fields only in the client or UI: this is wrong because the server still transmits sensitive data to the caller
- Reusing the internal `UserRecord` shape as the API contract: this is wrong because fields like `password`, `ssn`, or `internal_note` leak unless explicitly excluded
- Returning different unknown-route or error bodies by code path: this is wrong because route probing and failure details can reveal internal behavior

## Quick Verification
```bash
# Confirm secure route allowlisting or fixed not-found handling exists
rg -n 'RouteEntry|dispatch_route|build_not_found|"\{"error":"not found"\}"' .

# Find likely unguarded full-record JSON builders that may expose sensitive fields directly
rg -n 'snprintf\s*\(|sprintf\s*\(' . | rg '"(password|ssn|internal_note|token|secret|email)"'

# Find direct serialization from internal record fields into API responses
rg -n 'users?\[[^]]+\]\.(password|ssn|internal_note|email)|->(password|ssn|internal_note|email)' .

# Build and run tests with common C toolchain entry points across project types
sh -c 'if [ -f Makefile ] || [ -f makefile ]; then make && (make test || true); elif [ -f CMakeLists.txt ]; then cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build && ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure; else cc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -o /tmp/verify_c $(find . -maxdepth 3 -name "*.c" ! -path "./build/*" ! -path "./.git/*") && /tmp/verify_c 1 || true; fi'
```

# Prevent information exposure through APIs

## What This Skill Does
Reduces information exposure in APIs by removing unused endpoints, replacing generic entity serialization with explicit response views/DTOs, and enforcing strict, schema-based response shapes so that only allowed fields are ever returned to clients, even when internal objects contain sensitive data.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Endpoint returns full database/entity objects (e.g., `res.json(user)` directly) | Introduce explicit DTOs/response mappers and return only whitelisted fields |
| Debug/legacy/admin endpoints exist that dump large objects or lists | Remove them, or hard-disable with a generic status (e.g., `410` with no body) |
| Generic helpers serialize arbitrary objects (e.g., `serializeEntity(entity)`) | Replace with per-endpoint/per-use-case DTO factories that expose minimal data |
| Responses (including errors) have no defined schema and may include extra fields | Define JSON schemas with `additionalProperties: false` and validate responses before sending |
| Multiple endpoints expose different views of the same entity | Define per-endpoint field allow-lists and shared filters; add tests that assert disallowed fields never appear |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Detect and refactor API responses that serialize full internal objects into minimal, explicit response models.
- Add schema-based validation (e.g., Ajv in Node.js) to reject responses that contain unexpected or sensitive fields.
- Introduce endpoint-specific field allow-lists and shared filters to enforce least-privilege exposure across endpoints.

### Cannot Do
- Cannot design full business-level authorization rules (who is allowed to see what) beyond field-level whitelisting.
- Cannot guarantee no information exposure from non-HTTP channels (logs, traces, metrics, message queues) unless those are explicitly handled in code.
- Cannot fix performance or versioning issues caused by schema changes; human judgment is needed for API evolution and client compatibility.

## Gotchas
- Returning internal models “for convenience”: Mapping directly from database/domain models to JSON without a whitelist is risky; always use explicit DTOs or filters even if models “look safe” today, because new fields may be added later and silently exposed.
- Over-trusting client-side hiding: Relying on the front-end to hide sensitive fields (e.g., not rendering them) is unsafe; once the backend sends a field, any client or attacker can read it from the raw response.
- Loose schemas: Defining JSON schemas but leaving `additionalProperties: true` (or omitted) still allows accidental sensitive fields to leak; to prevent that, set `additionalProperties: false` and validate every response, including errors.

## Quick Verification
```bash
# 1. Hit a previously vulnerable endpoint and inspect fields
curl -sS "http://localhost:3000/api/user?username=alice" | jq

# Expectation: response only contains explicitly whitelisted fields
# (e.g., id, username, email, role) and never passwordHash, ssn, apiKey, etc.

# 2. Try to force extra/sensitive fields into a response (during dev/test)
# For example, temporarily add passwordHash to the payload before sendUserProfile()
# and confirm Ajv (or equivalent) rejects it with a schema error.

# 3. Probe for removed/disabled debug endpoints
curl -i "http://localhost:3000/api/admin/all-users-debug"

# Expectation: receives a non-200 with generic status (e.g., 410) and empty body,
# or the route no longer exists (404) with no bulk data in the body.
```

# Prevent information exposure through APIs

## What This Skill Does
Reduces information exposure in APIs by replacing "return full object" patterns and generic serializers with explicit, minimal response shapes, enforcing per-endpoint schemas (including errors), and aligning returned fields with authorization rules. It also removes dead/unused endpoints to shrink attack surface, ensuring clients can't extract sensitive or internal data by calling APIs directly.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| API handler returns `asdict()` / ORM model / full object directly | Introduce a per-endpoint response mapper that only returns needed, non-sensitive fields |
| Endpoint returns more fields than documented or includes secrets (passwords, API keys, SSNs, tokens, internal flags) | Define a minimal response model and strip/deny sensitive or undocumented fields before serialization |
| API uses a generic serializer (e.g., `.to_dict()`, `.schema()`, auto-JSON) for responses | Replace with explicit serializers or view-model builders that project only allowed fields |
| No explicit response schema exists (especially for error responses) | Define and enforce response schemas, rejecting or removing unexpected keys and invalid types |
| Responses differ based on user role/permissions | Add role/authorization-aware field whitelists and ensure only allowed fields reach the client |
| Endpoint or route is no longer used or is "temporarily disabled" | Remove the handler or return a minimal generic 404/410 without internal details |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Identify and refactor patterns where APIs return full database records or domain objects directly.
- Introduce explicit per-endpoint response builders / DTOs and central sensitive-field lists.
- Add or tighten response schemas (including errors) and basic schema validation hooks.
- Implement whitelist-based field filtering by endpoint and/or role.
- Suggest removal or hard-disable of unused or debug endpoints that expose internal details.

### Cannot Do
- Infer business-specific authorization rules or which fields are legally/compliantly sensitive without hints from code or comments.
- Guarantee no data exposure from third-party libraries, proxies, or layers not visible in the project.
- Configure infrastructure-level protections (API gateway redaction, WAF rules, logging scrubbing) beyond code changes.
- Rewrite entire API designs or versions; focuses on hardening existing handlers and serializers.
- Automatically align with external specs (OpenAPI, GraphQL schema) if they're missing or inconsistent; needs developer confirmation.

## Gotchas
- Assuming client-side filtering is enough: Hiding fields in the UI does not protect against direct API calls; responses themselves must be safe before serialization.
- Over-relying on "blacklist" removal of sensitive fields: It's easy to forget to add new sensitive attributes. Prefer explicit per-endpoint/role whitelists or schemas as the primary control.
- Forgetting error and fallback paths: Handlers may leak internal messages, stack traces, or raw records in error responses; define and validate schemas for errors too.

## Quick Verification
```bash
# 1. Run tests (adjust command to your project)
pytest -k "api or information_exposure or user_profile" -q

# 2. Manually hit a previously vulnerable endpoint
curl -i http://localhost:5000/user/1

# Confirm the JSON does NOT contain:
# - password_hash
# - ssn
# - api_key
# - any undocumented/internal fields

# 3. (If schemas added) Run schema or type checks
mypy . || true
pytest -k "schema or response_validation" -q

# 4. Probe removed/deprecated endpoints
curl -i http://localhost:5000/internal/debug-user/1
# Expect 404/410 with minimal, generic body and no internal details
```

# Prevent information exposure through APIs

## What This Skill Does
This skill reduces API data exposure by replacing full-object or database-shaped responses with endpoint-specific response objects, enforcing per-endpoint field allow-lists and response schemas, and rejecting unregistered operations. Use it when handlers serialize entities directly, return overly broad error details, or leave obsolete endpoints callable.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| An endpoint serializes a full entity, record, or ORM model directly | Apply this fix |
| A response includes fields not required by that endpoint, including nested sensitive fields | Replace with an endpoint-specific response object or explicit field mapping |
| A route, operation, or handler is callable without an explicit registry or allow-list | Add an allow-list check and reject unregistered operations |
| Success or error payloads are built dynamically without contract checks | Enforce a per-endpoint response schema before sending |
| The code already returns only approved fields and validates response shape | No action needed |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Replace direct serialization of domain objects with endpoint-specific DTOs, records, or explicit maps
- Add per-endpoint allow-lists for callable operations and approved response fields
- Validate success and error payloads to reject unexpected or missing fields

### Cannot Do
- Decide business-safe fields without application context or API contract requirements
- Prevent exposure from unrelated issues such as authorization failures or insecure logging
- Guarantee all framework-level serializers, plugins, or reflection-based mappers are fully constrained without inspecting their configuration

## Gotchas
- Removing fields only in one code path: sensitive data often still leaks through error payloads, nested objects, or alternate handlers
- Using generic `ObjectMapper` or framework auto-serialization on entities: future model changes can silently expand exposed fields
- Keeping obsolete endpoints undocumented instead of deleted or blocked: hidden routes are still callable and still leak data

## Quick Verification
```bash
# Compile and run the sample app
javac AppVulnerableCode.java && java AppVulnerableCode alice

# Confirm sensitive fields are not present in the fixed response
java AppFixPythonCode alice | grep -E '"password"|"passwordHash"|"ssn"'
# Expect no output

# Confirm only approved fields are returned
java AppFixPythonCode alice
# Expect JSON with only allowed fields such as id and username

# Confirm unknown operations are rejected in code paths that use an allow-list
# Example expectation: FORBIDDEN / operation not allowed
```

# Prevent Information Exposure Through APIs

## What This Skill Does
This skill reduces information exposure in TypeScript APIs by replacing broad object returns and generic serialization with endpoint-specific response mappers, explicit field allowlists, and strict outbound schema validation for both success and error payloads. It also limits attack surface by replacing automatic route exposure with an explicit approved route manifest.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| A handler returns a database/entity/internal object with `res.json(...)`, `return ...`, or `JSON.stringify(...)` | Map to a new endpoint-specific response object that includes only approved fields |
| A response is built from a full object and filtered only on the client | Move filtering to the server and enforce an endpoint field allowlist before serialization |
| Outbound API payloads or error payloads have no strict schema | Add endpoint-specific strict schemas and validate the final mapped payload before sending |
| Routes are auto-discovered, auto-bound, or every handler/controller is exposed | Replace with a single explicit route manifest that registers only approved method/path pairs |
| Code already maps narrow response DTOs, validates strict outbound schemas, and exposes only approved routes | No action needed |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Replace full-object API responses with endpoint-specific mappers in TypeScript code
- Add strict outbound response validation using per-endpoint schemas for success and error payloads
- Convert broad route registration to an explicit allowlist-based manifest

### Cannot Do
- Decide business-level data classification without clear endpoint requirements
- Guarantee third-party middleware, proxies, or logging layers do not leak sensitive data elsewhere
- Infer a correct public response contract when the application has no defined API behavior

## Gotchas
- Reusing input or database schemas for responses: these are often broader than the public contract and can leak internal fields
- Validating before mapping: this checks the wrong shape; validation must run on the final outbound payload
- Keeping helper serializers like `JSON.stringify(user)` or `res.json(userRecord)`: these bypass field allowlists and can reintroduce leaks

## Quick Verification
```bash
# Confirm secure response mapping / allowlist / schema enforcement exists
rg -n "to[A-Z].*Response|map[A-Z].*Response|pickFields|enforceResponseSchema|\\.strict\\(\\)|z\\.object\\(" .

# Find unguarded dangerous API responses that may serialize full internal objects
rg -n "res\\.json\\((?!enforceResponseSchema\\(|to[A-Z].*Response\\(|map[A-Z].*Response\\().*\\)|JSON\\.stringify\\((?!to[A-Z].*Response\\(|map[A-Z].*Response\\().*\\)" .

# Find broad or automatic route exposure patterns that should be replaced with an approved manifest
rg -n "fs\\.(readdir|readdirSync)|require\\(.*controllers|autoload|auto.?register|router\\[[\"']use[\"']\\]|app\\[[\"']use[\"']\\]" .

# Build TypeScript project
npx tsc --noEmit

# Run project tests if present
npm test
```

results.title: ASD-STIG requirements
results.text:
## V-222393 [medium]:
__The application must associate organization-defined types of security attributes having organization-defined security attribute values with information in storage.__

Without the association of security attributes to information, there is no basis for the application to make security related access-control decisions.

Security attributes are abstractions representing the basic properties or characteristics of an entity (e.g., subjects and objects) with respect to safeguarding information.

These attributes are typically associated with internal data structures (e.g., records, buffers, files) within the information system and are used to enable the implementation of access control and flow control policies, reflect special dissemination, handling or distribution instructions, or support other aspects of the information security policy.

One example includes marking data as classified or FOUO. These security attributes may be assigned manually or during data processing but either way, it is imperative these assignments are maintained while the data is in storage. If the security attributes are lost when the data is stored, there is the risk of a data compromise.

Classify the system hosting the application with default classification.  Treat all unmarked data at the highest classification as the overall hosting system is classified.  If there is no classification, mark system high.

## V-222417 [low]:
__The application must notify System Administrators and Information System Security Officers when accounts are created.__

Once an attacker establishes access to a system, the attacker often attempts to create a persistent method of re-establishing access. One way to accomplish this is for the attacker to simply create a new account. Notification of account creation is one method for mitigating this risk. A comprehensive account management process will ensure an audit trail which documents the creation of application user accounts and notifies administrators and Information System Security Officers (ISSO) exists. Such a process greatly reduces the risk that accounts will be surreptitiously created and provides logging that can be used for forensic purposes.

To address access requirements, many application developers choose to integrate their applications with enterprise-level authentication/access/auditing mechanisms that meet or exceed access control policy requirements. Such integration allows the application developer to off-load those access control functions and focus on core application features and functionality.

## V-222422 [low]:
__The application must notify System Administrators and Information System Security Officers of account enabling actions.__

Once an attacker establishes access to a system, the attacker often attempts to create a persistent method of re-establishing access. One way to accomplish this is for the attacker to simply enable an existing account that has been previously disabled. Notification when account enabling actions occur is one method for mitigating this risk. A comprehensive account management process will ensure an audit trail which documents the enabling of application user accounts and notifies administrators and Information System Security Officers (ISSO) exists. Such a process greatly reduces the risk that accounts will be surreptitiously created and provides logging that can be used for forensic purposes.

To address access requirements, many application developers choose to integrate their applications with enterprise-level authentication/access/auditing mechanisms that meet or exceed access control policy requirements. Such integration allows the application developer to off-load those access control functions and focus on core application features and functionality.

## V-222426 [medium]:
__The application must enforce organization-defined discretionary access control policies over defined subjects and objects.__

Discretionary Access Control allows users to determine who is allowed to access their data. To mitigate the risk of unauthorized access to sensitive information by entities that have been issued certificates by DoD-approved PKIs, all DoD systems (e.g., networks, web servers, and web portals) must be properly configured to incorporate access control methods that do not rely solely on the possession of a certificate for access. Successful authentication must not automatically give an entity access to an asset or security boundary. Authorization procedures and controls must be implemented to ensure each authenticated entity also has a validated and current authorization. Authorization is the process of determining whether an entity, once authenticated, is permitted to access a specific asset. Information systems use access control policies and enforcement mechanisms to implement this requirement.

Access control policies include identity-based policies, role-based policies, and attribute-based policies. Access enforcement mechanisms include access control lists, access control matrices, and cryptography. These policies and mechanisms must be employed by the application to control access between users (or processes acting on behalf of users) and objects (e.g., devices, files, records, processes, programs, and domains) in the information system.

This requirement is applicable to access control enforcement applications (e.g., authentication servers) and other applications that perform information and system access control functions.

results.title: Use client-side validation to detect malicious behavior
results.text:
Since client-side validation mechanisms are easy to bypass, they cannot be relied upon for security. However, it is recommended to ensure that client-side validation procedures and server-side validation procedures enforce identical rules. In doing so, you can expect that server-side validation should not fail.

Under these conditions, a server-side input validation failure can be used as a signal of data tampering. __Such a failure should be seen as a security-relevant incident__, and should be logged appropriately.

Additionally, the system can decide to enforce further security restrictions. For example, the account can be locked, or the associated privileges revoked.

For more details on detecting suspicious behavior and acting upon such events, see the [OWASP AppSensor project](https://www.owasp.org/index.php/OWASP_AppSensor_Project).

results.title: ASD-STIG requirements
results.text:
## V-222602 [high]:
__The application must protect from Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities.__

XSS attacks are essentially code injection attacks against the various language interpreters contained within the browser. XSS can be executed via HTML, JavaScript, VBScript, ActiveX; essentially any scripting language a browser is capable of processing.

XSS vulnerabilities are created when a website does not properly sanitize, escape, or encode user input. For example, "&lt;" is the HTML encoding for the "<" character. If the encoding is performed, the script code will not execute.

There are 3 parties involved in an XSS attack, the attacker, the trusted and vulnerable website, and the victim. An attacker will take advantage of a vulnerable website that does not properly validate user input by inserting malicious code into any data entry field.

When the victim visits the trusted website and clicks on the malicious link left by the attacker, the attacker's script is executed in the victims browser with the trust permissions assigned to the site.

There are several different types of XSS attack and the complete details regarding XSS cannot be described completely here.

To address the issue of XSS, web application developers must escape, encode or otherwise validate all user input that is processed and output by the web server. They should also use web templates or a web development framework that provides the capability to encode or otherwise validate user input.

Examples of XSS vulnerabilities can be obtained from the Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP) website.
  
The site is available by pointing your browser to https://www.owasp.org.

## V-222604 [high]:
__The application must protect from command injection.__

A command injection attack is an attack on a vulnerable application where improperly validated input is passed to a command shell setup in the application. The result is the ability of an attacker to execute OS commands via the application.

A command injection allows an attacker to execute their own commands with the same privileges as the application executing.

The following is an example of a URL based command injection attack.

Before alteration:
http://sitename/cgi-bin/userData.pl?doc=user1.txt

Example URL modified: 
http://sitename/cgi-bin/userData.pl?doc=/bin/ls|

The result is the execution of the command "/bin/ls" which could allow the attacker to list contents of the directory via the browser.

The following is a list of functions vulnerable to command injection sorted according to language.  

Language Functions/Characters

- C/C++  - system(), popen(), execlp(), execvp(), ShellExecute(), ShellExecuteEx(), _wsystem()
- Perl - system, exec, `, open, |, eval, /e
- Python - exec, eval, os.system, os.popen, execfile, input, compile
- Java - Class.forName(), Class.newInstance(), Runtime.exec()

## V-222606 [medium]:
__The application must validate all input.__

Checking the valid syntax and semantics of information system inputs (e.g., character set, length, numerical range, and acceptable values) verifies that inputs match specified definitions for format and content. Software applications typically follow well-defined protocols that use structured messages (i.e., commands or queries) to communicate between software modules or system components. 

Structured messages can contain raw or unstructured data interspersed with metadata or control information. If software applications use attacker-supplied inputs to construct structured messages without properly encoding such messages, then the attacker could insert malicious commands or special characters that can cause the data to be interpreted as control information or metadata. 

Consequently, the module or component that receives the tainted output will perform the wrong operations or otherwise interpret the data incorrectly. Prescreening inputs prior to passing to interpreters prevents the content from being unintentionally interpreted as commands. Input validation helps to ensure accurate and correct inputs and prevent attacks such as cross-site scripting and a variety of injection attacks.

Absence of input validation opens an application to improper manipulation of data. The lack of input validation can lead immediate access of application, denial of service, and corruption of data.

Invalid input includes presence of scripting tags within text fields, query string manipulation, and invalid data types and sizes.

When an application validates input, it will only execute provided input after it has evaluated the input, validated the input and determined the data is in an expected format, and content is not extraneous or malformed.

Comprehensive application security testing and code reviews are required to ensure the application is not vulnerable to input validation vulnerabilities.

Application security code reviews should be conducted during the development phase to find and address input validation errors. When code reviews are not possible, fuzz testing can be performed on the application to attempt and identify vulnerable data input fields.

## V-222607 [high]:
__The application must not be vulnerable to SQL Injection.__

SQL Injection is a code injection attack against database applications. Malicious SQL statements are inserted into an application data entry field where they are submitted to the database and executed. This is a direct result of not validating input that is used by the application to perform a command or execute an action.

Successful attacks can read data, write data, execute administrative functions within the database, shutdown the DBMS, and in some cases execute OS commands.

Best practices to reduce the potential for SQL Injection vulnerabilities include:

Not using concatenation or replacement to build SQL queries.

Using prepared statements with parameterized queries that have been tested and validated not to be vulnerable to SQL Injection.

Using stored procedures that have been tested and validated not to be vulnerable to SQL Injection.

Escaping all user supplied input.

Additional steps to prevent SQL Injection can be found at the OWASP website:

https://www.owasp.org/index.php/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet

## V-222609 [high]:
__The application must not be subject to input handling vulnerabilities.__

A common application vulnerability is unpredictable behavior due to improper input validation. This requirement guards against adverse or unintended system behavior caused by invalid inputs, where information system responses to the invalid input may be disruptive or cause the system to fail into an unsafe state.

Data received from the user should always be suspected as being malicious and always validated prior to using it as input to the application.

Some examples of input methods:

- Forms Data
- URL parameters
- Hidden Fields
- Cookies
- HTTP Headers or anything in the HTTP request
- Client data entry fields

Items to validate:

- Out of range values/Boundary 
- Data length 
- Validate types of characters allowed
- Whitelist validation for known good data input while denying all other input.

Other recommendations include: 

- Using drop down menus for lists
- Validating input on the server, not on the client.

If validating on the client, also validate on the server:

- Using regular expressions to validate input
- Using HTML filter libraries that implement input validation tasks.

results.title: Sanitize Content Before Sending to Memcache (OWASP ASVS 5.0)
results.text: Sanitizing content before sending it to memcache is crucial in preventing injection attacks, which can compromise application security and data integrity. To secure your Memcached implementation, you must first review your application to identify all input points by analyzing how data is gathered, processed, and transmitted into the cache. Once these points are mapped out, implement strict input validation to guarantee that only legitimate data adhering to expected data types, lengths, and formats is processed. Next, apply robust sanitization techniques using language-specific functions or libraries to remove or encode any potentially dangerous characters before they hit the cache. Furthermore, if your Memcached interactions involve any form of query language, always utilize parameterized queries to eliminate the risk of injection attacks. Finally, sustain this security posture through continuous monitoring and regular testing to catch fresh vulnerabilities and verify that your validation and sanitization measures remain fully effective.

# Always perform input validation on a server

## What This Skill Does
This skill fixes improper input validation in Go by ensuring untrusted request or user input is normalized and validated on the server before it reaches business logic or sensitive APIs, logging validation failures with consistent security fields, and returning a single generic error message so callers do not learn which validation rule failed or what internal processing occurred.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Untrusted input reaches business logic or file/system APIs without prior validation | Add a dedicated server-side validation function and call it before processing |
| Input is only checked in the browser, client, or CLI before being sent | Treat it as untrusted and enforce the same checks again on the server |
| Validation code returns rule-specific or internal error details to callers | Replace with one generic error message and keep detailed causes in server-side logs |
| Validation failures are rejected but not logged consistently | Add a separate logging helper that records timestamp, source IP, fixed event description, and error code |
| Code already normalizes, validates server-side, logs failures, and returns generic errors | No action needed |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Add server-side validation for type, length, format, range, emptiness, and allowed characters
- Normalize input before validation, such as trimming and canonicalizing file paths
- Add separate validation-failure logging and generic caller-facing error handling

### Cannot Do
- Infer the correct validation rules for every business field without application context
- Guarantee safety if other code paths still call dangerous APIs with unvalidated input
- Replace authorization, output encoding, or parameterized queries, which solve different problems

## Gotchas
- Reusing detailed validation errors in responses: this leaks which rule failed or exposes internal file/system behavior
- Validating before normalization: checks can be bypassed if whitespace, alternate forms, or cleaned paths are handled later
- Logging validation failures inline with response text: this often mixes internal detail into caller-facing errors instead of keeping logs separate

## Quick Verification
```bash
# Confirm a server-side validation helper exists
rg -n 'func\s+validate[A-Za-z0-9_]*\s*\(' .

# Confirm validation-failure logging exists with a fixed event description
rg -n 'input validation failure|logValidationFailure\s*\(' .

# Find unguarded dangerous file-read calls that may bypass validation
rg -n 'os\.(ReadFile|Open|OpenFile)\s*\(' .

# Find caller-facing detailed error construction that should be generalized
rg -n 'fmt\.(Sprintf|Errorf)\("error:\s*%v"|errors\.New\(.+failed|http\.Error\s*\(.+err' .

# Build and test all Go packages
go build ./... && go test ./...
```

# Always Perform Input Validation on a Server

## What This Skill Does
This skill fixes improper input validation in Python by ensuring every server-controlled entry point validates untrusted input before parsing, conversion, persistence, or business logic. Apply it when request parameters, JSON fields, form values, CLI arguments, message payloads, or other external inputs are trusted too early. The fix centralizes reusable validation, rejects invalid or unexpected input early, logs validation failures with bounded structured details, and returns only a generic error message to callers.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Request handlers, CLI entry points, workers, or helpers use external input before checks | Add a server-side validator and call it before any `int()`, `float()`, indexing, persistence, or business logic |
| The same field or payload shape is validated in multiple places | Centralize validation in a reusable function such as `validate_quantity()` and reuse it across all entry points |
| Validation failures return detailed rule information to the client | Replace with one generic response such as `{"error": "Invalid input."}` and keep specifics only in logs |
| Validation failures are not logged or logs include raw attacker input | Add structured logging with timestamp, source IP if available, event, and error code; avoid raw untrusted values |
| Code already validates type, required fields, length, range, format, and allowed values before use | No action needed |

## Boundaries

### Can Do

# Use the correct HTTP methods for making state-changing operations

## What This Skill Does
This skill fixes CSRF-prone request handling where Python code lets `GET` or `HEAD` perform state changes such as create, update, delete, logout, token invalidation, or balance transfers. It moves mutating logic behind `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE`, adds an explicit request-method gate before parsing input or calling mutators, and ensures unsupported methods fail with `405 Method Not Allowed` so read-only requests stay free of side effects.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| A Flask/Django/FastAPI/Python HTTP handler uses `GET` or `HEAD` and then calls a mutating function or writes session/database state | Move the mutation to a `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE` route and reject `GET`/`HEAD` with `405` |
| A handler reads mutation input from `request.args`, query strings, or URL parameters for an action like transfer, logout, delete, or update | Replace query-driven mutation with form or body input on a non-GET method |
| Code parses request data before checking `request.method` | Add method gating first, then parse input, then run business logic |
| The framework route is already limited to `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE` and `GET`/`HEAD` handlers are read-only | No action needed |
| A state-changing endpoint is exposed via hyperlink, image URL, prefetchable URL, or redirect target | Replace it with a form or API call using the intended non-GET method |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Refactor Python request handlers so `GET` and `HEAD` are read-only
- Add explicit method checks such as `if request.method != "POST": abort(405)`
- Separate read handlers from mutating handlers and route writes through `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE`

### Cannot Do
- Guarantee CSRF safety by method changes alone; mutating non-GET routes may still need CSRF tokens or origin checks
- Infer full business semantics for choosing between `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, and `DELETE` without application context
- Prove the absence of side effects hidden inside downstream helpers, ORMs, caches, or audit hooks without code review

## Gotchas
- Allowing `HEAD` because "it has no body": wrong, `HEAD` must follow the same no-state-change rule as `GET`
- Only changing the route decorator and leaving shared mutating logic callable from a read path: wrong, `GET` code paths can still trigger writes indirectly
- Returning a redirect instead of `405` for wrong methods on a mutating endpoint: wrong, the unsafe method should be rejected explicitly and state must remain unchanged

## Quick Verification
```bash
# Confirm method gating or non-GET route restrictions exist in Python handlers
rg -n 'request\.method\s*!=\s*"(POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE)"|abort\(405\)|methods\s*=\s*\[(?:[^]]*"(POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE)"[^]]*)\]' .

# Find likely unguarded dangerous patterns: GET/HEAD routes or query args feeding state-changing actions
rg -n '@app\.route\(.*methods\s*=\s*\[[^]]*"(GET|HEAD)"[^]]*\].*\)|request\.args\.get\(|request\.GET\[|request\.query_params|request\.method\s*==\s*"GET"' .

# Build + test with generic Python toolchain commands
python -m compileall .
python -m pytest -q
```

# Use the correct HTTP methods for making state-changing operations

## What This Skill Does
Aligns HTTP methods with their intended semantics so that state-changing actions (create/update/delete, logout, transfers, etc.) are never performed via GET/HEAD. This preserves the security assumption that safe methods are side‑effect free, simplifies CSRF protection (tokens/origin checks on non‑GET only), and prevents attackers from triggering sensitive actions via cross-site GET requests, links, or prefetch/caching.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| A GET/HEAD handler performs logout, balance reset, or any data mutation | Move the state-changing logic to a POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE handler; keep GET/HEAD strictly read-only or return 405 |
| A resource creation (signup, transfer, create item) is exposed on GET or mixed into another method | Expose creation via POST only; ensure body parsing and validation run only on POST for that action |
| An update/delete is implemented via GET or POST for an existing resource | Map full/partial updates to PUT/PATCH and deletions to DELETE; remove mutation from GET and, where practical, from POST |
| Shared business logic can mutate state regardless of HTTP method | Add a method parameter/guard so helpers reject calls when method is GET/HEAD; call this from all mutation helpers |
| CSRF middleware is configured to protect GET routes or not used consistently | Centralize a “method requires CSRF” helper that treats GET/HEAD as safe and apply CSRF checks only to non‑safe methods, after verifying GET/HEAD truly never change state |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Detect and refactor endpoints where GET/HEAD perform state changes (logout, resets, writes).
- Reorganize route handlers so creates use POST and updates/deletes use PUT/PATCH/DELETE, keeping GET/HEAD read-only.
- Introduce method-aware helper functions and CSRF policies that enforce “GET/HEAD are safe” as a strict invariant.

### Cannot Do
- Cannot add full CSRF protection (tokens/origin checks) by itself; it only prepares the method model CSRF relies on.
- Cannot fix other CSRF-related issues such as missing SameSite cookies, weak session secrets, or XSS.
- Cannot change external clients or third-party integrations that depend on legacy semantics without human review and migration planning.

## Gotchas
- Keeping the old GET route and silently redirecting to a mutating POST handler: still dangerous if the redirect causes the POST to run with user cookies; instead, make GET non-mutating and return 405 or a confirmation view that uses POST.
- Allowing “harmless” counters or logging side effects on GET: these can break assumptions for caching, idempotency, and CSRF tooling; all observable state changes must be on non‑GET methods.
- Applying CSRF protection to POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE while leaving some state changes on GET: gives a false sense of security because attackers will target the unprotected GET endpoints instead.

## Quick Verification
```bash
# 1) Grep for obvious state-changing GET routes (logout/reset/etc.)
grep -R --line-number -E "app\.get\(.+(logout|delete|reset|update|create| transfer|balance)" .

# 2) Run a crafted GET against formerly mutating endpoints and confirm no state change
curl -i -b cookies.txt "https://your-app.example/logout"
curl -i -b cookies.txt "https://your-app.example/reset-balance"

# 3) Confirm state changes only occur via non-GET methods
curl -i -X POST   -b cookies.txt "https://your-app.example/logout"
curl -i -X POST   -b cookies.txt "https://your-app.example/reset-balance"
curl -i -X PATCH  -b cookies.txt "https://your-app.example/profiles/alice"
curl -i -X DELETE -b cookies.txt "https://your-app.example/profiles/alice"

# 4) If using Node/Express example, run the fixed app and simulate the method guard
node app_fix_original_code.js GET   # should print "Method not allowed" for logout
node app_fix_original_code.js POST  # should perform logout
```

# Use the Correct HTTP Methods for State-Changing Operations

## What This Skill Does
This skill fixes CSRF exposure caused by treating `GET` or `HEAD` as state-changing operations. In JavaScript applications, it finds handlers, route definitions, and helper functions where safe methods perform mutations such as logout, session invalidation, create/update/delete actions, or persistent state changes, then moves those operations to `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE`. It also adds method classification and fail-closed guards so safe methods stay read-only and non-safe methods remain eligible for CSRF protection.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| A `GET` or `HEAD` route logs out users, destroys sessions, resets data, deletes data, or updates state | Move the mutation to `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE`; return `405` or no-op on `GET`/`HEAD` |
| Route registration is centralized or can be wrapped | Add a route-definition guard that rejects mutating handlers bound to `get` or `head` |
| The code classifies request methods for security checks | Explicitly treat only safe methods as read-only and require CSRF protection for all other methods |
| A `GET` or `HEAD` request includes mutation-like inputs such as `action=logout` or unexpected bodies | Reject the request and do not perform any state change |
| Code already keeps `GET`/`HEAD` read-only and protects non-safe methods with CSRF validation | No action needed |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Change JavaScript route handlers and helper functions so mutations use `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE`
- Add method guards such as `isSafeMethod`, `methodRequiresCsrfProtection`, or route-registration validation
- Add explicit rejection for `GET` or `HEAD` calls that attempt logout, session destruction, updates, deletes, or other mutations

### Cannot Do
- Implement complete CSRF token issuance and client integration for every framework automatically
- Infer business intent when a handler has mixed read and write behavior without code evidence
- Guarantee protection if state changes still occur in downstream code paths triggered by nominally read-only handlers

## Gotchas
- Allowing logout on `GET` because it seems harmless: logout changes authentication state and is still a CSRF-sensitive mutation
- Moving a route from `GET` to `POST` but leaving helper functions to mutate on `GET`: direct calls, CLI paths, tests, or background invocations can still preserve the bug
- Treating all non-`GET` methods as automatically protected: changing the verb is not enough unless non-safe methods also go through CSRF validation

## Quick Verification
```bash
# Confirm secure method-classification or guard helpers exist
rg -n "isSafeMethod|methodRequiresCsrfProtection|ensureNonSafeMethodForMutation|rejectSuspiciousSafeMethodMutations|defineRoute" .

# Find unguarded dangerous patterns where GET/HEAD still appears to perform mutations
rg -n "app\.(get|head)\s*\([^)]*(logout|reset|delete|destroy|update|invalidate)|router\.(get|head)\s*\([^)]*(logout|reset|delete|destroy|update|invalidate)|req\.session\.destroy\s*\(|\.destroy\s*\(|\b(balance|state|session|user)\b\s*=" .

# Build if a build script exists, then run tests if present
npm run build --if-present && npm test --if-present
```

# Use the Correct HTTP Methods for State-Changing Operations

## What This Skill Does
This skill fixes CSRF-prone designs where C# applications let browser-triggerable `GET` or `HEAD` requests perform state-changing work such as logout, create, update, delete, or transfer actions. It enforces correct HTTP method semantics by binding read-only behavior to `GET`/`HEAD`, moving mutations to `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE`, adding centralized method policy and guard checks where dispatch paths are shared, and preserving anti-forgery validation for unsafe browser-authenticated requests.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| A controller action, minimal API, helper, or request handler performs mutation from `GET` or `HEAD` semantics | Apply this fix |
| ASP.NET Core code uses broad route bindings like `[Route]`, shared dispatch, or custom method parsing that can bypass verb-specific attributes | Add a centralized `HttpMethodPolicy`/`HttpMethodGuard` and reject disallowed methods before mutation |
| Logout is exposed through `GET` | Replace with `POST` only and reject `GET` |
| Browser-authenticated `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE` endpoints exist without anti-forgery validation | Keep the unsafe verb and add anti-forgery validation; do not convert the action to `GET` |
| Endpoint already uses exact verb binding, read-only `GET`/`HEAD`, and guarded mutation paths | No action needed |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Change C# endpoint declarations and handler code so state changes do not execute via `GET` or `HEAD`
- Add or centralize verb-allow rules with `HttpMethodPolicy`, `HttpMethodGuard`, or explicit ASP.NET Core verb attributes
- Separate query-only code paths from command/mutation code paths and preserve anti-forgery checks on unsafe browser methods

### Cannot Do
- Infer full business intent for ambiguous endpoints without code clues, route names, or handler behavior
- Guarantee CSRF protection if the application uses unsafe ambient authentication but anti-forgery middleware or token plumbing is missing
- Fix non-HTTP invocation paths such as message queues, cron jobs, or internal method calls unless they explicitly model HTTP method semantics

## Gotchas
- Adding anti-forgery to `GET` instead of fixing the verb: this is wrong because `GET` must remain read-only; anti-forgery is not a substitute for correct method semantics
- Relying only on route attributes in shared handlers: this is wrong when custom dispatch or utility methods can still call mutation logic without checking the actual method
- Treating logout as harmless `GET`: this is wrong because logout changes authenticated session state and is browser-triggerable

## Quick Verification
```bash
# Confirm centralized guard/policy or explicit secure verb bindings exist
rg -n --glob '*.cs' 'HttpMethodPolicy|HttpMethodGuard|EnsureAllowed|IsMethodAllowed|\[Http(Post|Put|Patch|Delete)\]|\[ValidateAntiForgeryToken\]'

# Find dangerous GET-style state-changing patterns that likely bypass the fix
rg -n --glob '*.cs' '(\[HttpGet[^\]]*\][\s\S]{0,300}(Delete|Remove|Update|Create|Transfer|Logout|SignOut|Save))|(ProcessGetTransferRequest)|(MapGet\s*\([^)]*(delete|remove|update|create|transfer|logout|signout))'

# Build all discovered C# projects or solutions
find . \( -name '*.sln' -o -name '*.csproj' \) -print0 | xargs -0 -n1 dotnet build

# Run tests for all discovered test projects; if none exist, command does nothing
find . -name '*Test*.csproj' -o -name '*Tests*.csproj' -print0 | xargs -0 -r -n1 dotnet test
```

## What This Skill Does
This skill fixes CSRF-prone request handling where Java code lets safe HTTP methods such as `GET` or `HEAD` trigger server-side state changes. It adds a single method-to-action policy, normalizes and validates the incoming method before business logic runs, rejects unknown or disallowed methods instead of falling back, and ensures logout and other mutations only happen through state-changing methods such as `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE`.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| A Java handler, controller, servlet, filter, CLI dispatch method, or router performs logout, create, update, delete, or submit logic without checking `httpMethod` / `request.getMethod()` | Apply this fix |
| `GET` or `HEAD` reaches code that changes fields, session state, stored data, or invokes delete/update operations | Move the action to `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE` and reject `GET` / `HEAD` before state changes |
| Logout is reachable with `GET` or `HEAD` | Require `POST` for logout and reject safe methods |
| Method parsing uses raw strings, defaults unknown methods, or falls through to an action | Normalize method names, validate against an allowlist, and reject unknown methods |
| Code already enforces a shared allowlist where `GET` / `HEAD` are read-only and state-changing actions require intended methods | No action needed |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Add or tighten Java method checks before state-changing business logic runs
- Introduce a shared action-to-allowed-method mapping using core Java types like `EnumMap` and `EnumSet`
- Reject unknown, malformed, or disallowed methods without falling back to a default action

### Cannot Do
- Add complete framework-specific routing changes for every Java web stack automatically
- Prove all side effects are gone if state changes happen indirectly in downstream services or database triggers
- Replace CSRF tokens or same-site cookie protections where those are still needed for allowed state-changing requests

## Gotchas
- Checking only for `GET` and allowing everything else: this is wrong because unknown or unexpected methods may still reach state-changing code
- Enforcing methods after mutation logic starts: this is wrong because session or data changes may already have happened before rejection
- Allowing logout over `GET` for convenience: this is wrong because logout changes server-side session state and can be triggered cross-site

This skill fixes CSRF-prone request handling where TypeScript applications allow `GET` or `HEAD` to trigger server-side state changes such as updates, deletes, submits, or logout. It moves state-changing behavior to `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE`, and adds centralized method validation so mismatched methods are rejected with `405 Method Not Allowed` before business logic runs.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| A `GET` or `HEAD` route performs create, update, delete, submit, or logout work | Change the endpoint to `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, or `DELETE` and reject `GET`/`HEAD` with `405` |
| Request handling is spread across controllers, services, or route files | Add a centralized method policy or middleware that normalizes `req.method` and enforces allowed methods before business logic |

| Code already uses read-only `GET`/`HEAD` and state changes only on `POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE` | No action needed |

### Can Do
- Convert state-changing Express or similar TypeScript routes from `GET`/`HEAD` to the correct HTTP methods
- Add method normalization and enforcement that rejects mismatched methods before handlers execute
- Identify obvious logout, update, create, delete, and submit flows that should not be reachable by `GET`

## V-222393 [medium]:
__The application must associate organization-defined types of security attributes having organization-defined security attribute values with information in storage.__

Without the association of security attributes to information, there is no basis for the application to make security related access-control decisions.

Security attributes are abstractions representing the basic properties or characteristics of an entity (e.g., subjects and objects) with respect to safeguarding information.

These attributes are typically associated with internal data structures (e.g., records, buffers, files) within the information system and are used to enable the implementation of access control and flow control policies, reflect special dissemination, handling or distribution instructions, or support other aspects of the information security policy.

One example includes marking data as classified or FOUO. These security attributes may be assigned manually or during data processing but either way, it is imperative these assignments are maintained while the data is in storage. If the security attributes are lost when the data is stored, there is the risk of a data compromise.

Classify the system hosting the application with default classification.  Treat all unmarked data at the highest classification as the overall hosting system is classified.  If there is no classification, mark system high.

## V-222425 [high]:
__The application must enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.__

To mitigate the risk of unauthorized access to sensitive information by entities that have been issued certificates by DoD-approved PKIs, all DoD systems (e.g., networks, web servers, and web portals) must be properly configured to incorporate access control methods that do not rely solely on the possession of a certificate for access. 

Successful authentication must not automatically give an entity access to a restricted asset or security boundary.

Authorization procedures and controls must be implemented to ensure each authenticated entity also has a validated and current authorization.

Authorization is the process of determining whether an entity, once authenticated, is permitted to access a specific asset.

Information systems use access control policies and enforcement mechanisms to implement this requirement.

Access control policies include identity-based policies, role-based policies, and attribute-based policies.

Access enforcement mechanisms include access control lists, access control matrices, and cryptography.

These policies and mechanisms must be employed by the application to control access between users (or processes acting on behalf of users) and objects (e.g., devices, files, records, processes, programs, and domains) in the information system.

This requirement is applicable to access control enforcement applications (e.g., authentication servers) and other applications that perform information and system access control functions.

## V-222517 [medium]:
__The application must employ a deny-all, permit-by-exception (whitelist) policy to allow the execution of authorized software programs.__

Utilizing a whitelist provides a configuration management method for allowing the execution of only authorized software. Using only authorized software decreases risk by limiting the number of potential vulnerabilities.

The organization must identify authorized software programs and permit execution of authorized software. The process used to identify software programs that are authorized to execute on organizational information systems is commonly referred to as whitelisting.

Verification of whitelisted software can occur either prior to execution or at system startup.

This requirement applies to configuration management applications or similar types of applications designed to manage system processes and configurations (e.g., HBSS and software wrappers).

# Make authorization decisions using full context

## What This Skill Does
This skill fixes insufficient authorization checks caused by missing end-user context. It updates JavaScript code so business logic and downstream services receive an explicit `authContext` object with the minimum required authorization attributes such as `userId`, `permissions`, `roles`, `tenantId`, and ownership scope. It also standardizes fail-closed behavior when context is missing, malformed, expired, incomplete, or untrusted, and ensures propagated claims are verified before use.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Authorization functions accept only `userId`, `documentId`, `action`, or similar partial inputs | Refactor the function to accept a canonical `authContext` object and make the decision from that full context plus resource attributes |
| Business/model/service-layer code re-fetches permissions or infers them from global/request state | Pass normalized permission and scope data directly into the method instead of re-fetching or inferring it |
| Downstream authorization relies on JWT or forwarded claims | Verify claims with `jwt.verify(...)`, validate required fields, audience, and freshness, then map only trusted claims into `authContext` |
| Client-supplied headers/body fields are used directly for authorization | Reject untrusted raw fields and authorize only from validated server-side or integrity-protected context |
| Code already passes normalized context and denies when required fields are missing | No action needed |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Refactor JavaScript authorization helpers and business methods to accept an explicit `authContext`
- Add normalization and fail-closed validation for required authorization fields
- Verify propagated JWT claims before downstream authorization decisions

### Cannot Do
- Invent the correct authorization policy when required permissions, roles, or scopes are undefined by the application
- Guarantee end-to-end trust across services without real signing keys, issuer rules, and deployment configuration
- Fix unrelated authentication flaws such as weak login, session handling, or broken identity proofing

## Gotchas
- Passing only `userId` as "context": this is still incomplete if the decision also depends on permissions, tenant, roles, ownership, or request scope
- Normalizing missing permissions to an empty array and then treating that as sufficient context: missing required claims should deny authorization, not silently downgrade checks
- Trusting decoded but unverified JWT data with `jwt.decode(...)`: decoded claims are not integrity-checked and must not drive authorization

## Quick Verification
```bash
# Confirm a canonical authorization context or verifier exists
rg -n "function\s+(normalizeAuthContext|authorizeDocumentAccess|verifyDownstreamAuthContext)\b|jwt\.verify\(" .

# Find likely unguarded or partial authorization patterns that bypass full-context checks
rg -n "function\s+\w*authoriz\w*\([^)]*(action|documentId|userId)[^)]*\)|\b(authoriz\w*|readDocument|canDeletePost)\([^,)]*(documentId|userId|action)[^)]*\)|jwt\.decode\(" .

# Build + test using the project's available JavaScript toolchain
npm test || yarn test || pnpm test || bun test
```

# Make authorization decisions using full context

## What This Skill Does
This skill fixes insufficient authorization checks caused by missing actor or resource information. It updates Python code so protected operations receive one complete, server-derived authorization context object and evaluate access using both actor attributes and trusted resource attributes at the exact layer that returns or mutates protected data. It also preserves end-user context across service boundaries when downstream code performs the authorization check.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Protected function reads, returns, updates, or deletes sensitive data using only `document_id`, `user_id`, `username`, `role`, or request parameters | Apply this fix |
| Authorization inputs are scattered across multiple parameters or reconstructed from globals/session/request state | Replace with a single required immutable `AuthzContext`-style object |
| Authorization checks use client-supplied owner, tenant, or scope values instead of trusted server-side resource data | Load the target resource from a trusted source first and authorize against both actor and resource |
| A downstream service or repository makes the authorization decision | Forward end-user authorization context in a structured form and reconstruct it before the check |
| Code already requires full server-derived actor context and trusted resource context at the enforcement point | No action needed |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Refactor Python service, model, repository, and helper functions to require a complete authorization context input
- Replace partial authorization checks with checks that compare actor context to trusted resource attributes
- Add validation for missing or malformed authorization context and preserve end-user context across service calls

### Cannot Do
- Invent correct authorization rules, roles, tenant semantics, or ownership policy without evidence from the codebase
- Prove distributed callers actually authenticate or sign propagated context unless that mechanism already exists
- Guarantee security if other code paths still access the same protected resource without the required context

## Gotchas
- Passing only `user_id` or `role`: this is still incomplete because ownership, tenant, scopes, and other required attributes may be missing
- Trusting request JSON, headers, or query parameters for `owner`, `tenant_id`, or `role`: these are client-controlled and cannot replace server-derived authorization attributes
- Adding checks only in controllers: deeper service or repository functions may still be called directly and bypass authorization if they do not require context

## Quick Verification
```bash
# Confirm a required authz context or equivalent guard exists in protected code
rg -n "class AuthzContext|@dataclass\(frozen=True\)\s*class AuthzContext|def .*?\((ctx|authz_context|user): .*?, document_id: str\)" .

# Find likely unguarded dangerous access patterns that bypass full-context authorization
rg -n "def (fetch|get|read|update|delete)_[a-z_]*\((document_id|resource_id|user_id): .*?\):|return document\.content|\.content\s*=|DOCUMENTS\[[^\]]+\]" .

# Build + test using common Python toolchain commands; run what exists
python -m compileall .
pytest -q
python -m unittest discover
```

# Make authorization decisions using full context

## What This Skill Does
This skill fixes insufficient authorization checks caused by making access decisions without enough end-user context in the enforcing layer. In Node.js code, it replaces checks based only on `userId`, request presence, or ambient state with explicit `authContext` inputs that carry trusted identity, permissions, tenant, and resource-scoping data; it also ensures downstream services validate signed context and that missing or malformed context denies access.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Authorization logic accepts only `userId`, request data, or a truthy caller value | Refactor the enforcing function to accept an explicit `authContext` object and validate required fields before deciding access |
| Service/model/data-layer code needs permissions but reads them from request input or inferred state | Build `authContext` from a trusted server-side lookup such as `getPermissionsForUser(userId)` and deny if lookup fails |
| A separate service or tier makes the authorization decision | Propagate only needed claims in a signed token, verify with `jwt.verify(...)`, validate required claims, then convert to internal `authContext` |
| Authorization already validates explicit identity, permissions, tenant/resource scope, and fails closed on missing data | No action needed |
| Code uses ambient globals like `req.user`, thread-local state, or process-wide context inside reusable authorization helpers | Pass the needed context as a function argument instead of relying on implicit state |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Refactor Node.js authorization helpers and service functions to take explicit `authContext` parameters
- Add trusted permission-loading and normalization such as `buildAuthContext(userId, tenantId)`
- Add signed downstream context handling with `jsonwebtoken` verification and required-claim checks

### Cannot Do
- Invent correct authorization rules, roles, or resource ownership semantics that the application does not define
- Prove that an upstream identity source or permission store is trustworthy without project-specific evidence
- Secure systems that intentionally allow access without authentication or where business logic depends on unavailable domain context

## Gotchas
- Passing raw request claims straight into authorization: this is wrong because client-controlled fields can be altered and are not trusted permission data
- Using `jwt.decode(...)` or reading token payloads without `jwt.verify(...)`: this is wrong because integrity is not checked before authorization use
- Treating partial context as "good enough": this is wrong because missing fields like `tenantId`, ownership attributes, or permissions must cause deny-by-default

## Quick Verification
```bash
# Confirm explicit authorization context or trusted builders exist
rg -n "authContext|buildAuthContext|getPermissionsForUser|canReadDocument|jwt\.verify\(" .

# Find likely unguarded authorization-sensitive calls that still rely on incomplete context
rg -n "if\s*\(\s*userId\s*\)|getDocumentForUser\s*\(\s*userId\s*,\s*documentId|req\.(query|body)\.(roles?|permissions|tenantId)|jwt\.decode\(" .

# Build the project if a build script exists
npm run build --if-present

# Run tests if present; works for apps, libraries, CLIs, and services using npm
npm test --if-present
```

# Make authorization decisions using full context

## What This Skill Does
This skill fixes authorization flaws caused by making access decisions without the full end-user context. In C#, it replaces partial checks such as role-only decisions, `ClaimsPrincipal` lookups deep in the stack, or trusted `isAuthorized` flags with an explicit strongly typed authorization context that carries the required subject, permissions, tenant, ownership, and resource scope data. The receiving layer must recompute authorization where resource facts are available and fail closed if required context is missing or malformed.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Methods or service calls pass only `userId`, `role`, `callerRole`, or a boolean like `isAuthorized` | Introduce a strongly typed `AuthorizationContextData` parameter and pass explicit identity, permissions, and required scope values |
| Deeper layers read `ClaimsPrincipal`, `HttpContext`, or ambient request state directly | Move claim extraction to the entry point, normalize values once, and pass the resulting authorization context explicitly |
| Authorization depends on tenant, owner, account, project, or resource attributes | Include those exact inputs in the receiving-layer check and recompute authorization next to the resource facts |
| Cross-service or serialization boundaries drop end-user authorization details | Serialize and validate the minimal authorization context needed by the downstream decision point |
| Code already uses explicit context, validates required fields, and recomputes authorization in the receiving layer | No action needed |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Introduce a typed authorization context object and thread it through C# methods and service calls
- Replace ambient or partial authorization inputs with explicit subject, permission, and scope data
- Add fail-closed validation when identity, permissions, tenant, or ownership inputs are required

### Cannot Do
- Infer the correct authorization model when business rules for ownership, tenanting, or permission names are unknown
- Replace a full policy engine or redesign an application's entire identity architecture
- Guarantee secure authorization if downstream code still trusts caller-supplied approval flags or omits resource facts

## Gotchas
- Passing only `userId` or only `role`: this is still incomplete when the decision also depends on permissions, tenant, ownership, or action
- Reusing `ClaimsPrincipal` in deep layers: this keeps authorization dependent on ambient state and makes background jobs, libraries, and service boundaries inconsistent
- Treating missing scope as optional: defaulting to anonymous, default tenant, or caller identity turns malformed context into unintended access

## Quick Verification
```bash
# Confirm a typed authorization context is present
rg -n --glob '*.cs' 'class\s+AuthorizationContextData|record\s+AuthorizationContextData|CreateFromPrincipal\s*\(|RequireContext\s*\(' .

# Find likely unguarded ambient authorization usage or partial checks that bypass explicit context propagation
rg -n --glob '*.cs' 'IHttpContextAccessor|HttpContext\.User|Thread\.CurrentPrincipal|ClaimsPrincipal\.Current|callerRole|isAuthorized|alreadyAuthorized|FindFirst\s*\(|FindAll\s*\(' .

# Build all discovered C# projects/solutions
find . \( -name '*.sln' -o -name '*.csproj' \) -print0 | xargs -0 -I{} dotnet build "{}"

# Run tests for all discovered C# test projects/solutions
find . \( -name '*.sln' -o -name '*Tests.csproj' -o -name '*.Tests.csproj' \) -print0 | xargs -0 -I{} dotnet test "{}"
```

# Make authorization decisions using full context

## What This Skill Does
This skill fixes authorization flaws caused by making allow/deny decisions with incomplete information, such as only a user ID, only a role, only a tenant, or only a resource identifier. In Java code, it introduces a strongly typed immutable authorization context, passes that context and the target resource/action through every layer involved in access control, centralizes policy checks where full context exists, and makes missing or inconsistent data fail closed instead of falling back to allow.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Methods authorize or access protected data using only `userId`, `role`, `tenantId`, `documentName`, or similar partial values | Apply this fix |
| Services, repositories, or internal APIs assume an upstream layer already checked authorization | Add explicit `AuthorizationContext`, `Action`, and resource inputs, then re-check where full context exists |
| Authorization logic is spread across controllers, services, and helpers with inconsistent inputs | Replace with a shared authorizer that evaluates full subject + action + resource + tenant context |
| Downstream/internal service calls rely on caller trust, network location, DTO shape, or service identity alone | Require propagated end-user authorization context and deny when it is missing |
| Code already uses immutable typed context, explicit action/resource checks, tenant matching, and deny-by-default on missing inputs | No action needed |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Refactor Java authorization code to accept a typed immutable `AuthorizationContext`
- Add explicit `Action` and resource metadata inputs to authorization checks
- Change allow logic to deny by default when context is null, partial, or inconsistent

### Cannot Do
- Invent trusted user, tenant, role, or permission data that the application does not already authenticate or resolve
- Define business authorization policy that is not already implied by the code or requirements
- Guarantee security if some call paths still bypass the shared authorizer or protected service boundary

## Gotchas
- Passing raw request fields into `AuthorizationContext`: this is wrong because tenant, roles, and permissions must come from authenticated and trusted server-side data, not caller-controlled input
- Checking only `hasRole("ADMIN")` or only `hasPermission(...)`: this is wrong because authorization often also requires tenant match, resource ownership, sensitivity, workflow state, and exact action
- Making the check in the wrong layer: this is wrong because repositories or helpers often lack full resource and action context, which leads to partial-input allow decisions

## Quick Verification
```bash
# Confirm a typed authorization context or equivalent authorizer exists
rg -n --glob '*.java' 'record AuthorizationContext|class AuthorizationContext|class .*Authorizer|boolean isAllowed\s*\(' .

# Find likely unguarded protected-data access paths that bypass full-context authorization
rg -n --glob '*.java' 'public .*readDocument\s*\(\s*String\b|public .*process\s*\(\s*String\b|Files\.readString\s*\(|Files\.newInputStream\s*\(|Files\.readAllBytes\s*\(' .

# Find dangerous authorization patterns that use partial inputs only
rg -n --glob '*.java' 'hasRole\s*\(|hasPermission\s*\(|tenantId\s*\(|userId\s*\(' .

# Build and test with the detected Java toolchain
test -f pom.xml && mvn test
test -f build.gradle && ./gradlew test
test -f build.gradle.kts && ./gradlew test
```

# Make authorization decisions using full context

## What This Skill Does
This skill fixes authorization flaws caused by deciding access from incomplete inputs such as `role`, `userId`, request-local fields, or caller-supplied resource metadata. It standardizes authorization around one structured `AuthContext`, validates required fields before every decision, loads ownership and tenant data from authoritative application records, and preserves end-user, permission, delegation, and freshness data when context crosses service boundaries.

## Decision Table
| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Authorization checks use only `role`, `userId`, or request params/body fields | Replace the check with a single `AuthContext` passed into one authorization function |
| Resource ownership, tenant, or classification comes from request input | Load resource attributes from authoritative application data before authorizing |
| Context is forwarded across services or queues | Verify integrity/freshness, preserve subject/permissions/delegation metadata, and reject malformed or stale context |
| Required context fields are missing, empty, or malformed | Deny access by default before making the authorization decision |
| Code already validates full context and uses authoritative resource attributes | No action needed |

## Boundaries

### Can Do
- Refactor TypeScript authorization flows to accept one validated `AuthContext`
- Add schema validation and fail-closed checks before authorization decisions
- Replace caller-supplied resource metadata with authoritative loaded attributes

### Cannot Do
- Invent missing business rules for ownership, delegation, or tenant isolation
- Guarantee security of external identity tokens or service-to-service trust by itself
- Fix every authorization bug if the application lacks authoritative resource data sources

## Gotchas
- Rebuilding context from partial fields at lower layers: this reintroduces the same bug because services/repositories lose tenant, delegation, or permission data
- Trusting `ownerUserId`, `tenantId`, or classification from request input: caller-controlled metadata must not drive the authorization decision
- Validating shape but not freshness or integrity for forwarded context: signed-looking or well-formed context can still be stale, replayed, or tampered with

## Quick Verification
```bash
# Confirm a structured authorization context and validation path exist
rg -n --glob '*.ts' 'AuthContext(Schema)?|authorize\(|parseAuthContext\(|hasRequiredContext\(|isFullAuthContext\(' .
```
